llm.reply:
Three genes are linked to Li-Fraumeni syndrome. The first is NCBIGene:7157, tumor protein p53 [4]. The second is NCBIGene:11200, checkpoint kinase 2 [3]. The third is NCBIGene:1029, cyclin dependent kinase inhibitor 2A [1].

## TP53 as primary cause

The literature places the germline TP53 defect at the centre of the syndrome [19: "a cancer predisposition syndrome caused by a germline mutation of the TP53 gene on chromosome 17p13.1"]. It is inherited in a dominant fashion with high penetrance [19: "autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance with high penetrance"]. Loss of p53 function makes many cancers possible [19: "TP53 gene mutations cause the loss of function of p53, leading to downstream events permissive for development of various malignancies"].

## Tumour spectrum and variants

Typical tumours include sarcomas, early breast cancer, brain tumours and adrenocortical carcinoma [19: "soft tissue sarcomas, osteosarcoma, premenopausal breast cancer, brain tumors, and adrenal cortical carcinomas"]. One case report describes a specific exon 5 germline change [21: "the germinal mutation c.527G>T (p.Cys176Phe) on exon 5 of the TP53 gene"].

## Phenotypic heterogeneity

The same TP53 variant can present differently between and within families [22: "Phenotypic heterogeneity is present among different families affected by the same pathogenic variant in TP53 gene"]. Modifier variants in TP53-related genes, copy number changes and epigenetic effects may explain this variation [22: "polymorphic variants in TP53 gene or in TP53-related genes, copy number variations in particular regions, and/or epigenetic deregulation of TP53 expression"]. Registered trials include whole-body MRI surveillance of carriers [20: "Evaluation of Whole Body MRI for Early Detection of Cancers in Subjects With P53 Mutation"].

The retrieved records link three genes to Li-Fraumeni syndrome: NCBIGene:7157, tumor protein p53 [4]. NCBIGene:11200, checkpoint kinase 2 [3]. NCBIGene:1029, cyclin dependent kinase inhibitor 2A [1]. The disease record is named Li-Fraumeni syndrome [2].

## TP53 as cause

The literature describes the syndrome as caused by germline TP53 mutation, inherited dominantly [19: "caused by a germline mutation of the TP53 gene on chromosome 17p13.1"][19: "autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance with high penetrance"]. Loss of p53 function makes many cancers possible over a lifetime [19: "TP53 gene mutations cause the loss of function of p53, leading to downstream events permissive for development of various malignancies throughout life"]. The core tumours include sarcomas, breast and brain tumours, and adrenal carcinoma [19: "soft tissue sarcomas, osteosarcoma, premenopausal breast cancer, brain tumors, and adrenal cortical carcinomas"]. A Colombian case report confirmed a deleterious exon 5 germline variant [21: "(p.Cys176Phe) on exon 5 of the TP53 gene, a deleterious mutation described previously in tumoural tissues"].

## Phenotypic heterogeneity

Families carrying the same TP53 variant can show different phenotypes [22: "Phenotypic heterogeneity is present among different families affected by the same pathogenic variant in TP53 gene"]. Proposed modifiers include TP53-related gene variants and epigenetic changes [22: "polymorphic variants in TP53 gene or in TP53-related genes, copy number variations in particular regions, and/or epigenetic deregulation of TP53 expression"].

Li-Fraumeni syndrome (LFS) is a cancer predisposition syndrome caused by a germline mutation of the TP53 gene on chromosome 17p13.1. It has an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance with high penetrance. These patients have a very high lifetime cumulative risk of developing multiple malignancies
